the `BeforeDelete` implementation currently recalculates and updates DeletionGracePeriodSeconds:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/217a1c48531438ac2f4a202e828092a8ce19f4e6/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go#L105-L123

There are two things that need changing here (with unit tests that exercise each change):
* if the existing grace period is already less than zero we should delete immediately
* if the new period is less than zero we should clip to zero

```diff
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go
index 3e7ca85b761..7f90e5e18be 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go
@@ -103,9 +103,9 @@ func BeforeDelete(strategy RESTDeleteStrategy, ctx context.Context, obj runtime.
 		// 2. Delete the object from storage.
 		// If the update succeeds, but the delete fails (network error, internal storage error, etc.),
 		// a resource was previously left in a state that was non-recoverable.  We
-		// check if the existing stored resource has a grace period as 0 and if so
+		// check if the existing stored resource has a grace period <= 0 and if so
 		// attempt to delete immediately in order to recover from this scenario.
-		if objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() == nil || *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() == 0 {
+		if objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() == nil || *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() <= 0 {
 			return false, false, nil
 		}
 		// only a shorter grace period may be provided by a user
@@ -113,10 +113,13 @@ func BeforeDelete(strategy RESTDeleteStrategy, ctx context.Context, obj runtime.
 			period := int64(*options.GracePeriodSeconds)
 			if period >= *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() {
 				return false, true, nil
+			} else if period < 0 {
+				// clip to zero
+				period = 0
 			}
 			newDeletionTimestamp := metav1.NewTime(
 				objectMeta.GetDeletionTimestamp().Add(-time.Second * time.Duration(*objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds())).
-					Add(time.Second * time.Duration(*options.GracePeriodSeconds)))
+					Add(time.Second * time.Duration(period)))
 			objectMeta.SetDeletionTimestamp(&newDeletionTimestamp)
 			objectMeta.SetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds(&period)
 			return true, false, nil
```

> @michaelgugino @liggitt
> Maybe add non-negative integer verification on the client side, and then crop it to 0 elsewhere.
> This ensures that the API documentation is correct, and that existing persisted data containing negative values can be handled correctly

Current conforming clients don't send the negative value, so there's not much to change there.  Cropping to 0 is what I'm saying we shouldn't do, we should reject the value at the API.  Most likely, the user intent was 'use pod default' as that's what the delete/drain command help text specifies.

If we want to still accept the API call, then we should drop the field and default to nil instead.  This would allow users to shorten the time if they choose after the call succeeds.

Hi 👋 Friendly reminder that code freeze is end of the day (Pacific timezone) today!

Here's what I think we should do moving forward to fix this:

- Add validation in the API to ensure negative values are rejected
- If a negative value is already set, ignore it and use the default grace period rather than clipping to 0.

However, this proposal might be a behaviour change, and so it'd need a more detailed release note than as currently written.

This PR clips negative values to 0, which I think is incorrect, but it's probably the closest to the current behaviour for negative values. If a negative value is currently set, I believe it should always get replaced with the minimum grace period (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98866#discussion_r582361382).

@rphillips @michaelgugino @liggitt wdyt?

Is there a summary of the behavior we saw across dockershim, containerd, cri-o for how it handled receiving a negative value?

The provided value was passthrough from kubelet if I recall, and only overridden to be 'now' when we do eviction.
Just following up, the kubelet -> cri flow sets a minGracePeriod of 2s unless explicitly overriden by the override (eg in eviction)

/milestone clear

I think this is too big of a change to land 1wk before test freeze. Let's aim for merging this early in 1.22 and consider backporting.

/retest

As per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102025 I think when a user provides a negative deletion time it should be equal to 1 seconds, to be consistent and backwards compatible.  I'm concerned that tightening validation is a breaking change to a v1 api here.

> As per #102025 I think when a user provides a negative deletion time it should be equal to 1 seconds, to be consistent and backwards compatible. I'm concerned that tightening validation is a breaking change to a v1 api here.

That sounds reasonable at first glance. A couple questions:
* Which fields are you envisioning that applying to?
* At what point in the request are you envisioning the `if x < 0 { x = 1 }` translation happening?

These are the fields I see, and the points I could imagine doing the translation at:

* Probe#TerminationGracePeriodSeconds
  * in the API as an overriding defaulter on read
  * in the kubelet when reading the termination grace period
* PodSpec#TerminationGracePeriodSeconds
  * in the API as an overriding defaulter on read
  * in the API pod strategy when processing delete requests
* ObjectMeta#DeletionGracePeriodSeconds
  * in the API as an overriding defaulter on read
  * in the API rest handler when processing delete requests
* DeleteOptions#GracePeriodSeconds
  * when decoding DeleteOptions
  * in the storage delete handler

@liggitt How about both - on update (going into etcd) and out to users?  The negative value is very clearly unspecced, and any consumer reading negative and doing something out of bounds would prefer a correct value.  I can't see how a client (kubelet, namespace controller, etc) who sees 1 instead of -1 would be worse off.  We also want to be write repairing.

> I can't see how a client (kubelet, namespace controller, etc) who sees 1 instead of -1 would be worse off.

The multi-server skew case could cause problems for fields which are immutable (Probe#TerminationGracePeriodSeconds or PodSpec#TerminationGracePeriodSeconds
inside a pod) or required to be monotonically decreasing (metadata.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds)

immutable scenario:

1. Object is persisted with negative value in TerminationGracePeriodSeconds  field
2. Client reads from 1.22 server that replaces the negative value with 1 on read
3. Client changes an unrelated field and writes to a 1.21 server
4. 1.21 server rejects request because an immutable field was changed

metadata.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds scenarios:

* update: [stomped by old DeletionGracePeriodSeconds server-side](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.21/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/update.go#L131-L134); no multi-server skew issue
* delete: if a client read a negative-normalized-to-1 metadata.deletionGracePeriodSeconds from a 1.22 server and copied it into DeleteOptions sent to a delete call made to a 1.21 server, the 1.21 server would reject it in the `only a shorter grace period may be provided by a user` check. practically, I think this would only apply to pods, and I'm not aware of first-party clients that copy from metadata.deletionGracePeriodSeconds into deleteoptions

> The multi-server skew case could cause problems for fields which are immutable

To solve the multi-server skew issue, the change could be rolled out over 2 releases:
 * First release: 
     * Treat negative as 1 in delete path (pod/strategy.go, apiserver delete.go)
     * Allow delete with grace period 0 even if metadata period is negative (apiserver delete.go). This allows kubelet to delete pods.
     * Relax validation of immutable fields to allow it to be set to 1 if it was previously negative. This allows us to update read path in the next release. All consumers would also need to be able to handle this change in a sane manner.
 * Second release:
     * Treat negative as 1 in read path (defaulting or conversion)
     * Returning an error on Pod create could break things like Deployment updates. But if we update defaulting, then I think we won't hit this issue.

While we're on the topic of pod termination period, this was another problematic scenario where we set grace period = 0: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74372. At the time we didn't go through with changing it because we were concerned about the potential impact to pod deletion time, but maybe we can revisit again.

> Allow delete with grace period 0 even if metadata period is negative (apiserver delete.go). This allows kubelet to delete pods.

Neither this change nor 102025 should prevent kubelet from deleting pods.  The rule of 0 is disallowed is ONLY as a default deletion value on pod.spec (DELETE with 0 is still valid).

> Neither this change nor 102025 should prevent kubelet from deleting pods. The rule of 0 is disallowed is ONLY as a default deletion value on pod.spec (DELETE with 0 is still valid).

 I think that was saying we could fix the "delete with 0 is disallowed because it technically increases an existing negative objectmeta grace period" bug in release 1 as well

I don't think we should disallow anything other than negative values.
The two release rollout makes sense to me

> I think that was saying we could fix the "delete with 0 is disallowed because it technically increases an existing negative objectmeta grace period" bug in release 1 as well

My brain hurts on this one, but I think I agree then.

Dawn was mentioning she thought there was a reason for allowing 0 as the default on a pod, but the ones she remembered were latency related, which are roughly the same arguments those against allowing some garbage collection to happen after pod is deleted in etcd, except worse (force deleting a pod has the largest possible impact on background kubelet load).  Once context cancelling is tested in #102344 it's likely that total termination latency will come down significantly on moderate loaded clusters.

> First release:
>  - Treat negative as 1 in delete path (pod/strategy.go, apiserver delete.go)
>  - Allow delete with grace period 0 even if metadata period is negative (apiserver delete.go). This allows kubelet to delete pods.
>  - Relax validation of immutable fields to allow it to be set to 1 if it was previously negative. This allows us to update read path in the next release. All consumers would also need to be able to handle this change in a sane manner.


@liggitt PTAL

/remove-priority important-longterm

/lgtm
/approve

issue_context.title: Force deleting pods not working after deletionGracePeriodSeconds set to a negative value
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
Some k8s client tried to evict a pod by setting negative value for deletionGracePeriodSeconds. But all eventual delete calls (and force-delete calls) made by kubelet, pod-garbage-collector, etc were not able to delete that pod, because apiserver doesnt allow deletionGracePeriodSeconds to be increased once it is set. So force-delete (which set it to 0) doesn't take effect when it's already negative. Not even kubectl is able to call delete with negative grace-period. But curl with an even more negative grace-period value worked.


**What you expected to happen**:
force-delete works.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

**Anything else we need to know?**:
I think the issue is in the code below

```
	if objectMeta.GetDeletionTimestamp() != nil {
		// if we are already being deleted, we may only shorten the deletion grace period
		// this means the object was gracefully deleted previously but deletionGracePeriodSeconds was not set,
		// so we force deletion immediately
		// IMPORTANT:
		// The deletion operation happens in two phases.
		// 1. Update to set DeletionGracePeriodSeconds and DeletionTimestamp
		// 2. Delete the object from storage.
		// If the update succeeds, but the delete fails (network error, internal storage error, etc.),
		// a resource was previously left in a state that was non-recoverable.  We
		// check if the existing stored resource has a grace period as 0 and if so
		// attempt to delete immediately in order to recover from this scenario.
		if objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() == nil || *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() == 0 {
			return false, false, nil
		}
		// only a shorter grace period may be provided by a user
		if options.GracePeriodSeconds != nil {
			period := int64(*options.GracePeriodSeconds)
			if period >= *objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds() {
				return false, true, nil
			}
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/apiserver/blame/d4c9a195921609cf81e3e950beaf246f934e0f4c/pkg/registry/rest/delete.go#L96-L110

As the comment suggest, in phase 1, the `DeletionGracePeriodSeconds` was set to a negative value (meaning `DeletionTimestamp` was **in the past**), and in phase 2, `options.GracePeriodSeconds` has to be set even lower, otherwise, it will be considered as pending graceful deletion and not performing the immediate delete. 

I think there're two possible fixes. 

1. Consider not allowing setting `DeletionTimestamp` in the past (`DeletionGracePeriodSeconds` should be non-negative). In that case, we could convert `options.GracePeriodSeconds` to 0 if negative. 
2. Accept that `DeletionTimestamp` could be set in the past. In that case, in phase 2, we treat negative value of `objectMeta.GetDeletionGracePeriodSeconds()` the same as 0, and allow immediate delete. 

Thoughts?

No component in the system should ever treat the timestamp of DeletionTimestamp as authoritative.  In Kube, components are required to calculate the time period from when they observe the event in their local clock (i.e. 30s from now), not use the deletion timestamp.

A negative value of deletion grace period should be rejected by the apiserver as an invalid value (bad request / invalid field).

> A negative value of deletion grace period should be rejected by the apiserver as an invalid value (bad request / invalid field).

attempts to take a missing or positive deletion grace period negative should be rejected, I agree.

if a negative value is already persisted, I'd be inclined to allow a negative value in an update and clip to 0

As I mentioned in the PR, eviction is passing negatives through to the store: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L160

In kubectl, we specify the default value for GracePeriod is -1.  In the case of delete, we simply don't set the value in the deleteOptions we send to the API.  In the case of eviction, we send the -1 value, and that gets passed along to the store.

> In kubectl, we specify the default value for GracePeriod is -1. In the case of delete, we simply don't set the value in the deleteOptions we send to the API. In the case of eviction, we send the -1 value, and that gets passed along to the store.

I don't see the -1 getting sent to the eviction API. It looks like values < 0 result in a nil value being sent to the API:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4225e1f1cc38cec4986a79f10cecfbdb561e8d03/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/drain/drain.go#L136-L140

I would not expect the API to accept a negative value as-is.

> I would not expect the API to accept a negative value as-is.

Looks like you are correct.  Do the deletionOptions go through their own validation or through some kind of validation for the evict API?  The original bug report mentions 'evict' though it's not clear if the eviction API was used or not.

> Do the deletionOptions go through their own validation or through some kind of validation for the evict API? The original bug report mentions 'evict' though it's not clear if the eviction API was used or not.

ValidateDeleteOptions is called inside pod deletion, but did not check that the field was non-negative. I don't see any eviction-specific validation.
